newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania OSCE election coordinator quits.
newsitem.headline: Albania OSCE election coordinator quits.

text.p: The head of a European group monitoring the operation of Albania's elections has resigned for personal reasons, amid mounting concern over security and organisation of the June 29 poll.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said on Tuesday that Briton Brian Pridham, overall coordinator for the democratic and human rights arm of the OSCE in Albania, had returned to England.
OSCE spokesman Jeff Murray told Reuters that Pridham, who had been in Albania for just under a month organising foreign observers for the poll, would be replaced by another Briton, Tony Welch.
Murray denied that Pridham had quit over concerns about the handling of the operation.

The context of his departure -- days after OSCE officials voiced grave concern over security in parts of the country -- fuelled speculation that the poll might be delayed, but officials said they did not yet see any reason to hold up the vote.

The main parties have held peaceful campaign rallies outside the capital, but local tensions have mounted and obstacles facing international observers under Albania's current conditions have come closer into focus.
"A lot of the observers have had concerns about the state of affairs in the countryside but I am not aware of any decision to delay," a diplomatic source told Reuters.

Italy's defence undersecretary Massimo Brutti, visiting Tirana, also dismissed talk of a delay. "Only elections can bring us a credible government and only then the world will provide strong political, economic and financial support to Albania," he said.

A long delay would be politically controversial within Albania and beyond. Other Europeanm countries are determined to resume normal relations with Albania, which has been in a state of emergency since after mass riots earlier this year.

But diplomats have said there seems to be a consensus in the international community that a delay of one to three weeks, if forced by technical concerns about bringing off a fair and free ballot in Albania's mountainous terrain, may be accepted.
Murray said any decision to postpone the vote would only come from the Albanian government. "We do not have any intention of initiating a request to postpone the elections," he said.

The OSCE has said it will send more than 400 observers to watch the vote at some of the 4,500 polling stations. More than 100 experts are already in place, protected by a 6,500-strong Italian-led multinational force.

Swiss Gerard Stoudman, Warsaw-based director of the OSCE's election operations, said on Sunday the organisation would only send observers into Albania's most sensitive areas if it felt they would be safe.

Parts of Albania are still effectively out of government control and several bridges were damaged by explosions amid chaos and violence unleashed by popular outrage at the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes.

Potential problems range from practical matters like finding enough hotel beds in Europe's poorest country, which emerged from communist isolation only in 1990 , to fears that observers might be attacked by gangs and bandits in some areas.

Some observers, needing a military escort to travel, have been unable to reach districts they were due to visit. Certain places to the northeast and southeast of Tirana are no-go areas for some politicians, diplomats and journalists.
